explanations: terra: The ayah orders nonlife, first life, death, renewed life, and return to God, staging an entire succession whose later creation supplies the destination.

luna: The verse says they bought worldly life at the price of the Hereafter. The purchase turns the section’s deferred-value image into a failed exchange. | terra: ٱشْتَرَوُا۟ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا بِٱلْءَاخِرَةِ turns the choice of the earlier life over the later into an actual transaction.
terra: Whatever good is sent ahead is found with God later, so the apparent loss in the first time is preserved as the promised return.
terra: A petitioner asks only for this world and consequently has no share in the afterlife; 2:201 voices the fuller alternative.

luna: The supplication asks for good in this world and good in the Hereafter. It frames the two lives as distinct matters for which the worshipper asks what is good, echoing the section’s istikhara gloss. | terra: The prayer asks for good both in this world and in the afterlife, placing the two goods together rather than treating the first as the whole gift.
terra: Those who make the two-world prayer receive a share of what they earned, closing the choice staged by 2:200–201 with its outcome.
terra: At the point when believers ask when divine help will come, the answer says God's help is near, a concise response to felt delay.

luna: The verse says people may dislike something that is good for them and love something that is bad, while God knows and they do not. It supplies a specific reversal in how an outcome is judged, related to the section’s better choice. | terra: A disliked thing may be good and a loved thing bad because God knows the unseen outcome, showing why the better of two times cannot be judged from the first alone.
terra: A good loan to God is promised manifold repayment, using a present advance and guaranteed later increase as the section uses a deferred sale.

luna: A man is made to die for a hundred years and revived, yet estimates that he stayed a day or part of one. This makes elapsed time and the later return perceptibly different, as in the section’s end-time measure. | terra: After being made to die for a hundred years, the man estimates a day or part of a day; restored life exposes the gulf between elapsed and perceived time.
terra: The grain that yields seven ears and manifold kernels makes delayed divine multiplication visible as a crop growing beyond the original gift.

luna: The verse pictures a garden of palms and vines destroyed by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is old and has young children. This is a direct reversal of the section’s palm retaining its yield to the end: waiting for the final crop can still end in loss. | terra: A palm-and-vine garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is old and vulnerable, reversing the image of fruit preserved safely to the end.

luna: The creditor is told to grant respite to a debtor in hardship until ease. The section’s dictionary branch for ء خ ر gives a sale on credit as waiting for payment; this is the Quran’s concrete case of payment deferred.

luna: The verse begins with a debt contracted for a specified term and orders that it be written down. This supplies a concrete contractual form for the section’s deferred-sale image: payment is due later at an agreed time. | terra: A debt contracted to a named term must be written down, the Quran's clearest scene of deferred payment made secure by a documented agreement.
terra: When a scribe is unavailable, a received pledge secures the obligation described in 2:282, making concrete the section's claim that deferred payment remains guaranteed.

luna: The verse says only God knows the تأويل of the ambiguous verses. This may mean their ultimate reality rather than the section’s outcome sense, but it specifically marks interpretation as knowledge whose final reach is not presently available. | terra: تَأْوِيلِهِ can denote sought interpretation whose knowledge is contested or reserved to God; this semantic use cautions against reducing every taʾwīl to a visibly arrived event.
terra: The catalogue of immediate human desires ends by locating the good destination with God, moving evaluation from present attraction to final return.

luna: The verse asks whether it should tell the God-fearing of something better than worldly desires, then names gardens and God’s pleasure. It turns the section’s choice of the better of two matters into a direct world/Hereafter comparison.

luna: The verse says each soul dies only by God’s permission at a written term, then distinguishes those seeking the world’s reward from those seeking the Hereafter’s. It joins appointed timing to a choice between the two rewards. | terra: God gives from worldly reward to one who wants it and from afterlife reward to one who wants that, making two desired outcomes explicit alternatives.

luna: After the believers’ prayer, God gives them the reward of this world and the best reward of the Hereafter. This is a concrete instance of a later reward completing an earlier trial. | terra: God gives the believers worldly reward and the good reward of the afterlife, showing that an earlier gift can precede a better later one.
terra: Some fighters wanted this world and others wanted the afterlife, locating the two temporal choices inside one event and its immediate spoils.

luna: The deniers are warned not to mistake their reprieve for good; the respite increases their burden before humiliating punishment. This is a boundary on reading delay as a guaranteed benefit. | terra: Unbelievers mistake granted time for good, but their respite only increases sin; this is the clearest reversal of the section's equation between later and better.
terra: Those who withhold God's bounty think the withholding good for them, but its later embodiment as a collar exposes their mistaken comparison.
terra: Believers ask God to give what He promised through His messengers and not disgrace them on the later Day, voicing reliance on deferred assurance.
terra: The unbelievers' movement through the land is only a little enjoyment before their adverse lodging; 3:198 gives the opposite later hospitality.
terra: The Godfearing receive abiding gardens as hospitality from God, and what is with Him is better for the righteous.

luna: The command to return disputes to God and the Messenger is called خير and أحسن تأويلا. The verse joins the section’s “better” root to an explicit best outcome. | terra: Returning a dispute to God and the Messenger is called خَيْرٌۭ وَأَحْسَنُ تَأْوِيلًا, uniting what is better with what proves best in final outcome.
terra: Those who sell worldly life for the afterlife are promised a great reward, joining the section's sale image to deferred divine payment.

luna: The fighters ask to be delayed to a near term, then are told that worldly enjoyment is little and the Hereafter is better for the God-fearing. It joins the section’s named delay (ء خ ر) directly to its first/later valuation. | terra: The same ayah joins a plea for postponement, أَخَّرْتَنَآ إِلَىٰٓ أَجَلٍۢ, to the answer that the afterlife is better, directly uniting the section's delay and comparison.

luna: The verse asks who seeks the reward of this world, then says with God is the reward of both this world and the Hereafter. It places both temporal rewards under one owner, as in the section’s first/last pair. | terra: Whoever wants worldly reward is reminded that God possesses the reward of both this world and the afterlife, joining choice to the ownership stated in 92:13.
terra: Israel's covenant includes lending God a good loan followed by expiation and entry into gardens, another present advance with secured later payment.
luna: God is said to create people from clay and then set a term, with another specified term known to Him. This ties the beginning of human life to its appointed later limit.

luna: The verse says the Hereafter’s home is better for those mindful of God than worldly play and diversion. It develops the same comparative value of the later abode. | terra: وَلَلدَّارُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌۭ names the later abode as better for the Godfearing, an exact repeated Quranic judgment behind 93:4.
terra: The command to look at fruit when it first bears and when it ripens makes the interval between beginning and completed yield visible.

luna: The verse names date palms and says to give their due on the day of harvest, يوم حصاده. This ties the section’s date-palm branch to an explicitly appointed harvest and its yield. | terra: Date palms and varied crops bear fruit, and their due is paid on harvest day; the ayah supplies the section's concrete endpoint of fruit and harvest.

luna: Each community has an appointed term, and when it comes it cannot be delayed or advanced. This is a direct statement of a fixed endpoint for the section’s deferred-time image. | terra: When a community's term comes, it cannot be put back or brought forward by an hour, fixing the limit beyond which deferral is impossible.
terra: The people of Paradise say the messengers brought the truth as they are told to inherit the garden, a promised later home recognized at arrival.

luna: The verse asks whether people await anything but the Quran’s تأويل; when it arrives, those who forgot it confess that the messengers brought truth. A delayed outcome reverses their earlier denial. | terra: When the revelation's تَأْوِيل comes, those who forgot it confess that the messengers brought truth; taʾwīl here is the long-deferred event reaching fulfillment.

luna: The verse asks whether people feel secure from punishment arriving at duha while they play. The morning scene is a normal threshold before a later reckoning, adding a specific reversal to the section’s unfinished, bright day. | terra: Divine punishment may arrive ضُحًۭى while a town plays, using the same daylight threshold as 93:1 but turning its growing light into exposed vulnerability.
terra: وَٱلدَّارُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌۭ contrasts the later home with people repeatedly taking the goods of the nearer world.
terra: God progressively draws deniers toward their end from where they do not know, supplying the movement whose apparent respite is named in 7:183.
terra: God grants respite while His plan is firm, so temporal extension conceals rather than cancels the secured adverse outcome.
terra: God promises one of two groups while the believers want the easier one, exposing a choice between alternatives whose truly good result God determines.

luna: The captives are told that if God knows good in their hearts, He will give them better than what was taken from them and forgive them. This is a concrete later compensation for an earlier taking, using the section’s better-choice root. | terra: Captives are told that if God knows good in them He will give something better than what was taken, making loss now the prelude to a promised better grant.

luna: The verse asks whether people are satisfied with worldly life over the Hereafter, then calls worldly enjoyment in the Hereafter little. It directly reverses the section’s valuation. | terra: The question أَرَضِيتُم بِٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا مِنَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ exposes satisfaction with the nearer life as a bad exchange because its enjoyment is little.
terra: Promised gardens are followed by God's greater pleasure, so even the named later gift opens onto something described as greater.
terra: God's purchase of believers' lives and wealth for Paradise is a covenant-backed transaction whose price is paid in the later abode.
terra: The ayah combines universal return, وَعْدَ ٱللَّهِ حَقًّا, and God's beginning creation then repeating it, joining outcome, assurance, and second creation.

luna: The verse says that if God hastened evil for people as they hasten good, their term would already have been concluded. It makes the contrast between human haste and deferred divine timing explicit.

luna: Worldly life is likened to rain-fed plants that flourish, then become harvestable and turn to debris. Its growth-to-ending sequence gives a crop image for the section’s weighing of what comes later. | terra: When the earth's growth ripens and its owners think it is under their power, God's command comes by night or daylight and leaves it harvested bare.

luna: The deniers reject what they do not comprehend and whose تأويل has not yet come. This is a direct instance of the section’s outcome sense being unavailable before its time. | terra: They deny before knowledge encompasses it and وَلَمَّا يَأْتِهِمْ تَأْوِيلُهُۥ, so the eventual outcome has specifically not yet arrived.

luna: At the gathering, people think they stayed only an hour of a day before recognizing one another. Like 79:46, the end changes how the span before it is measured. | terra: At gathering, people feel they remained only an hour of the day, compressing the whole first interval once its outcome has arrived.
terra: Whether the Prophet is shown part of what is promised or dies first, the people still return to God; fulfillment is not confined to the addressee's first-life horizon.

luna: Each community has a term; when it arrives, it cannot be delayed or advanced even an hour. The verse repeats the section’s fixed-endpoint relation with an explicit measure of time. | terra: After 10:48 demands the promised event, this ayah says every community has a term which it can neither delay nor advance by an hour.

luna: The call to seek forgiveness is followed by a promise of good enjoyment until an appointed term and a reward for every possessor of bounty. This is provision granted over a bounded future interval.

luna: The punishment is delayed until a countable term, and the deniers ask what is holding it back. The verse makes postponement itself a challenge before the promised outcome. | terra: Postponing punishment to a counted period makes scoffers ask what holds it back; unlike the section's delayed gift, this secured later event is adverse.
terra: Those who want worldly life and its adornment are paid their works in full here, setting the immediate payment whose later result appears in 11:16.
terra: This ayah discloses the deferred outcome of 11:15's apparently complete worldly payment: they have nothing in the afterlife but the Fire.
terra: وَمَا نُؤَخِّرُهُۥٓ إِلَّا لِأَجَلٍۢ مَّعْدُودٍۢ says the coming Day is delayed only to a counted term, making postponement measured rather than uncertain.
terra: Prayer at the two ends of day and early night maps worship onto temporal boundaries rather than a single undifferentiated day.

luna: Yusuf’s father says God will choose him, teach him تأويل events, and complete His favor on Jacob’s family. The verse presents interpretation and favor as promised future outcomes. | terra: Joseph is promised instruction in taʾwīl and completion of favor near the beginning of his story; 12:100 later identifies the old dream's realized outcome.

luna: After Yusuf is sold into Egypt, the verse says God establishes him there and teaches him interpretation of events. The later station and knowledge follow his earlier vulnerable one, as the section’s own-life reading allows. | terra: At Joseph's establishment in Egypt, God says He will teach him taʾwīl and will prevail in His affair, an early stage whose distant result appears in 12:100.
luna: The prisoners ask Yusuf to explain their visions, using تأويل. Their dreams receive particular outcomes later, making this a concrete use of the section’s result/interpretation sense.
luna: Yusuf promises to explain the prisoners’ dreams before their food arrives. The same root sense of تأويل is explicitly attached to a meaning that will be disclosed before a near future event.

luna: The king’s dream joins fat and lean cows to green and dry ears; the next verses ask Yusuf for its interpretation and forecast stored grain. It introduces the crop-and-later-provision sequence. | terra: The king's vision of seven cows and seven ears is the image whose interpretation in 12:47–49 unfolds as a long scheduled sequence of harvest, storage, scarcity, and relief.
luna: The king’s interpreters call the dreams confused and say they do not know their تأويل. Their failed present reading contrasts with Yusuf’s later, specific account.
luna: After a period, the freed prisoner remembers Yusuf and offers to bring back the dreams’ تأويل. The verse stages delayed recall and interpretation; the king’s dream follows in verse 46.

luna: The king’s dream is restated as seven fat cows, seven lean cows, and green and dry ears before Yusuf explains it. These crop images make the later storage plan in verses 47–49 answer a specific dream.

luna: Yusuf’s plan says to sow for seven years and leave the grain in its ears except a little for eating. This is an explicit crop kept through its growing and harvest stages for a later need, close to the section’s palm fruit remaining until the final picking. | terra: Joseph tells people to sow for seven years and leave most grain in its ears, a harvest deliberately retained now for a later need.

luna: The stored grain is to carry Egypt through seven severe years. It shows what the previous verse’s harvest delay secures: provision held over for the lean period. | terra: Seven hard years will come after the years of sowing and consume the stored crop, making the deferred provision's purpose visible.

luna: After the seven lean years, a year of rain and pressing follows. The later relief completes the sequence of storing provision and receiving its yield afterward. | terra: Then a year of rain and pressing arrives, completing the dream's timed sequence with relief after preservation and scarcity.

luna: After Yusuf’s story of reversal and establishment, the verse says the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and fear God. It is another explicit statement of the section’s later-abode valuation.
luna: Yusuf welcomes his parents and family into Egypt in safety just before naming the fulfillment of his former dream. This is the reunion that precedes the delayed dream’s completion in verse 100.

luna: Yusuf calls the family’s arrival and bowing the تأويل of his earlier dream, which God has made true. This is the section’s lexical sense of an earlier matter reaching its later result. | terra: Joseph identifies the present fulfillment as تَأْوِيلُ رُءْيَٰىَ مِن قَبْلُ; a word and vision from long before have reached the outcome meant by the section's dictionary sense of taʾwīl.
terra: After the dream's fulfillment Joseph recalls being taught taʾwīl and asks to be joined with the righteous, placing interpretation within his life's reached outcome.
terra: وَلَدَارُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ خَيْرٌۭ repeats the better-later formula after directing attention to the outcomes of former peoples.
terra: Help comes only after the messengers' wait reaches an extremity, making delayed rescue no evidence that the divine promise has disappeared.
terra: Flood foam disappears while what benefits people remains in the earth, a concrete Quranic measure of transient appearance against lasting good.
terra: Worldly life is only a brief enjoyment when measured against the afterlife, repeating the scale used in 4:77.
terra: The promised garden has enduring fruit and shade, carrying the section's harvest image into the later abode where provision no longer expires.
terra: Whether the Prophet sees part of the promised outcome or dies before it, his task is delivery and God's is reckoning.

luna: The verse describes those who prefer worldly life over the Hereafter and turn others from God’s path. It supplies a concrete contrary preference. | terra: Those who prefer worldly life over the afterlife enact the very choice between first and later whose better term the section weighs.

luna: The messengers say God calls people to seek forgiveness and will defer them to an appointed term. It is a direct instance of respite with a later deadline. | terra: The messengers offer forgiveness and postponement to an appointed term, joining a favorable grant to explicit temporal deferral.

luna: The good tree gives its fruit at every season by its Lord’s permission. It is a specific recurring yield that helps a reader see the temporal pattern behind the section’s retained fruit. | terra: The good tree gives its fruit at every appointed season by its Lord's permission, a Quranic image of fruit remaining ordered by divine timing.

luna: God does not overlook wrongdoers; He only postpones them to a day when eyes stare. The verse makes the deferred reckoning explicit. | terra: God's apparent delay is not heedlessness: wrongdoers are postponed to a terrifying Day, reversing the section's favorable future while preserving its certainty.
terra: At the arrival of punishment, wrongdoers ask to be postponed to a near term; the request exposes the point at which a desired extension is no longer available.

luna: No community precedes its term or delays it. This states the boundary around postponement in the section’s timed promise. | terra: No community can precede its appointed term or delay it, pairing temporal advance and postponement as an unalterable measure.
terra: God knows both ٱلْمُسْتَقْدِمِينَ and ٱلْمُسْتَـْٔخِرِينَ, the precise opposition between advancing and coming later used to define الآخر in the section.

luna: When the mindful are asked what God sent down, they answer “good,” and the verse says the Hereafter’s home is better. It repeats the section’s ranking in a question-and-answer setting. | terra: The Godfearing answer that their Lord sent down good, and the ayah concludes that the home of the afterlife is better.

luna: Those who emigrated after being wronged are promised a good place in this world, while the reward of the Hereafter is greater. It is a specific present/later valuation tied to a real change of circumstance. | terra: وَلَأَجْرُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ أَكْبَرُ describes later reward as greater, closely paralleling both خَيْرٌ in 93:4 and the greater degrees of 17:21.

luna: If God seized people immediately for wrongdoing, none would remain, but He postpones them to an appointed term; when it arrives, they can neither delay nor advance it. This directly develops delay with a fixed endpoint. | terra: People are postponed to a named term, but when it arrives they cannot delay or advance it even an hour; every granted interval has a hard boundary.
terra: After creation, some people are returned to a frail age and lose former knowledge; a person's own later phase can therefore diminish rather than improve.

luna: What people have will perish, while what is with God remains; the patient are promised a better reward. This directly states the passing/remaining relation developed by the section’s later-time image. | terra: مَا عِندَكُمْ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقٍۢ distinguishes what runs out from what remains, explaining why a delayed divine good can be better.
terra: They preferred worldly life over the afterlife, making explicit the human selection that reverses the section's scale.

luna: Those who desire the immediate life are given some of it, then face Hell. This shows the limited near reward against the later reckoning. | terra: Whoever wants the immediate is given a hastened allotment and then Hell; 17:19 supplies the opposite choice and 17:21 compares their degrees.

luna: Whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as a believer has effort appreciated. It presents the other choice from verse 18 and its later outcome. | terra: Whoever wants the afterlife and strives for it has effort gratefully accepted, the deferred counterpart to 17:18's hastened share.
terra: كُلًّا نُّمِدُّ supplies both groups from the Lord's gift, preparing 17:21's comparison of how their outcomes differ.

luna: After noting differing ranks among people, the verse says the Hereafter is greater in degrees. It compares what comes later with distinctions in the present life. | terra: The statement that the afterlife is greater in degrees gives a second measure of the superiority expressed by خَيْرٌ in 93:4.

luna: Just measure is called better and أحسن تأويلا. The verse gives the section’s “outcome” sense a concrete ethical case: fair dealing leads to the better end. | terra: Honest measure is خَيْرٌۭ وَأَحْسَنُ تَأْوِيلًا; a transaction done rightly now is judged by its better eventual result.
luna: The answer to doubt about resurrection is the One who created people the first time. This gives the section’s beginning/following relation a direct first-creation context.

luna: On the day God calls people, they answer praising Him and think they remained only a little. The call at the end changes the scale of the time before it. | terra: When God calls and people respond with praise, they suppose they had remained only a little, linking awakening and retrospective compression.
terra: Iblis asks to be postponed until Resurrection Day so he can master Adam's descendants; the same delay form serves a hostile project rather than a secured good.
terra: The Prophet is directed to night worship in hope that his Lord will raise him to a praised station, a personally addressed better state still ahead.

luna: The sleepers estimate that they stayed a day or part of one, unaware of the long span before waking. This is a parallel in perceived duration to 79:46, though it concerns sleep rather than the Hereafter. | terra: The sleepers estimate a day or part of one after awakening; 18:25's much longer count makes this a worldly analogue to resurrection's compressed first life.
terra: The stated three hundred and nine years supply the objective duration that the sleepers of 18:19 experienced as only a day or less.

luna: The verse explicitly gives the alternatives of belief and disbelief to whoever wills, then states the fire’s consequence. The section’s خ ي ر dictionary branch includes leaving someone a choice between two matters; here the choice has a defined boundary.

luna: The garden is described as vines surrounded by date palms, with cultivated land between them. This supplies the particular palm-and-crop scene that the following verse says bore fruit. | terra: The parable begins with vineyards surrounded by date palms, supplying the fruit-bearing scene whose presumed permanence and collapse appear in 18:36–42.
luna: The two gardens yield their produce without loss, with a river between them. It makes the fruit-bearing garden in verse 32 a scene of provision before the later boast and ruin.
luna: Entering his garden, the owner says he does not think it will ever perish or that the Hour will come. His confidence in permanence is reversed when the garden is ruined in verse 42.

luna: The owner imagines that, if returned to his Lord, he will find something better than the garden. His claim uses خيرا and an end or return, but mistakes present prosperity for a guaranteed better outcome. | terra: The garden owner assumes his wealth will never perish and that, if returned, he will find an even better resort; his claim mimics the better-later promise without divine warrant.

luna: The companion hopes his Lord will give him a garden better than the owner’s and send a calamity on the present one. It gives a concrete contrast between current yield and a hoped-for later replacement. | terra: The believing companion says his Lord may give him a garden better than the other's and send ruin on the present garden, opposing warranted hope to boastful certainty.

luna: The owner’s fruit is surrounded and the garden lies collapsed, leaving him to regret what he spent. The fruitful scene’s later destruction makes the end of a crop-bearing garden visible. | terra: His fruit is encompassed and he wrings his hands over what he spent, showing a worldly crop whose expected future disappears.

luna: After the garden’s collapse, the verse says true protection belongs to God and names the best reward and outcome, خيرا ثوابا وخير عقبا. This joins the section’s outcome sense of ء و ل to its better-later valuation. | terra: After the garden's collapse, God's reward and outcome are declared better, distinguishing a true divine future from the owner's imagined one.
luna: Worldly life is like rain that grows plants before they dry and scatter as fragments. The verse makes a plant’s temporary yield a concrete contrast to the enduring good deeds named next.

luna: Wealth and children adorn worldly life, while lasting good deeds are better for reward and hope. The verse contrasts temporary present goods with what lasts. | terra: ٱلْبَـٰقِيَـٰتُ ٱلصَّـٰلِحَـٰتُ are better with the Lord in reward and hope than the adornments named earlier in the ayah.

luna: Moses sees a wall about to collapse, which Khidr repairs without taking a fee; verse 82 later explains the protected treasure beneath it. The scene sets up provision preserved for the orphans’ future.

luna: Khidr promises, سأُنَبِّئُكَ بتأويل, that he will explain later what Moses could not bear. The section’s dictionary sense of تأويل is an outcome or where a matter comes to; this verse makes the explanation itself deferred. | terra: سَأُنَبِّئُكَ بِتَأْوِيلِ promises a future explanation for what Moses could not await, and 18:82 supplies the wall's delayed-provision outcome.

luna: The boat is damaged before Khidr explains that a king would otherwise seize every intact boat. What first appears harmful has a protective later outcome, the same before/after pattern the section develops.

luna: Khidr says the child’s death is tied to what the parents would face and to God’s intended replacement, explained in the next verse. The row’s contribution is the painful first event whose later meaning is withheld.

luna: After the child’s death, God intends a replacement “better” in purity and affection. The section’s خ ي ر branch concerns choosing what is better; this is a painful first loss followed by a promised better outcome. | terra: The child's parents are to receive from their Lord a replacement better in purity and mercy; this promised substitution is explained only after the painful earlier event.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for ء خ ر includes a deferred due and fruit kept to the end of harvest; Khidr says the orphans’ treasure is held until they reach full strength, when they can recover it. The retained value is for a later, appointed time. | terra: The wall's تَأْوِيل includes treasure kept hidden until two orphans mature, a concrete provision delayed yet secured until its proper time.
terra: The Gardens are promised while unseen, and إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ وَعْدُهُۥ مَأْتِيًّۭا says the promise is itself certain to arrive.
terra: The Merciful extends the deluded until they see the threatened event; a longer first interval ends by exposing who has the worse station.
terra: Enduring good deeds are better in reward and خَيْرٌۭ مَّرَدًّا, a better place of return that recalls the section's definition of taʾwīl as return and destination.
luna: Moses is told that the staff will be returned to its former state, سيرتها الأولى, after appearing as a snake. The lexical “first” becomes a concrete before-and-after reversal.

luna: The appointment for the gathering is the Day of Adornment, with people gathered at duha. It gives the section’s named morning interval a specific appointed time. | terra: Moses fixes the encounter as an appointed day and requires the people to gather ضُحًۭى, joining the section's morning threshold to a scheduled fulfillment.
terra: Pharaoh's magicians refuse to prefer him over the signs and observe that his power ends with this worldly life; 20:73 states what is better and lasting.
terra: وَٱللَّهُ خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰ gives the converts' reason for accepting present punishment: God's forgiveness is better and more enduring.

luna: At the gathering, people whisper that they remained only ten days. It is another specific estimate of an earlier span as the final day arrives. | terra: At resurrection people whisper that they stayed only ten days, a first estimate refined further in 20:104.

luna: The most moderate of them says they remained only a day. This sharpens the previous estimate into the same end-time compression of life found in 79:46. | terra: The most discerning say the stay was only one day, intensifying the later life's contraction of all that came before.
terra: The punishment of the afterlife is more severe and more enduring, a direct reversal in which later is greater and lasting but not better for its recipient.
terra: A prior word from the Lord and a specified term prevent immediate judgment, so an earlier divine commitment governs when the later event arrives.
terra: The Prophet is told to glorify before sunrise, before sunset, and at the day's ends so that he may be satisfied, joining ordered times to the hoped-for رِضَا.

luna: The verse warns against coveting worldly adornment and calls the Lord’s provision better and more lasting. It connects the section’s future gift to enduring provision. | terra: The transient bloom of worldly life is tested against وَرِزْقُ رَبِّكَ خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰ, the Lord's provision that is better and more lasting.
terra: God fulfilled His promise to earlier messengers and saved them, presenting the later realization after the earlier word.
terra: As God began the first creation He will repeat it, and وَعْدًا عَلَيْنَآ إِنَّا كُنَّا فَـٰعِلِينَ makes that second beginning an expressly guaranteed promise.
terra: After clear warning, the Messenger says he does not know whether the promised event is near or far, preserving the promise while withholding its schedule.
terra: Human life and revived earth unfold through successive stages toward a named term and resurrection, making a person's own first and later phases visible.

luna: People ask for punishment to be hastened, but God will not fail His promise; a day with Him is like a thousand years by their count. It links delay to a radically different measure of the promised time. | terra: Those who demand punishment be hastened are answered that God never breaks His promise, directly separating apparent delay from failed assurance.
terra: After successive embryonic stages God brings the human being forth as another creation, establishing the first life before 23:15–16's death and resurrection.
terra: After that created life human beings will die, the boundary between the first creation of 23:14 and the raising in 23:16.
terra: After death people will be raised on Resurrection Day, completing the ordered first-life and second-life sequence.
terra: No community can precede its appointed term or postpone it, repeating the exact advance-and-delay boundary developed by the section.

luna: God asks how many years the people stayed on earth before the answer in verse 113. This sets up the section’s question of how a whole earlier life looks from its end. | terra: The resurrection question asks how many years the people stayed on earth, opening the temporal reckoning answered in 23:113–114.

luna: They answer that they stayed a day or part of a day. The compressed duration parallels the life reduced to an evening or duha in 79:46. | terra: They answer that they stayed a day or part of one, voicing from the later life the felt brevity of the first.

luna: God says they stayed only a little, had they known, then asks whether they thought they were created without purpose and would not return. The short first span is measured against return. | terra: The reply confirms that their stay was only little, had they known, completing the change of temporal scale begun in 23:112.
terra: Believers are told not to count an apparent evil as evil for them but as good, a communal instance of the first appearance being corrected by its eventual value.
terra: The ayah asks whether the threatened fate is better or the eternal garden promised to the Godfearing, explicitly choosing between two eventual outcomes.
luna: The verse says God brings the truth and the best تأويلا in answer to the opponents’ arguments. It uses the section’s named interpretation root for a later, decisive explanation.
terra: The One who begins creation and then repeats it also provides from heaven and earth, joining second creation to continuing provision.
luna: Moses says his Lord knows who will have the good outcome of the Home. This uses the section’s endpoint/result idea to frame the final outcome beyond a present dispute.

luna: Worldly enjoyment is contrasted with what is with God, which is better and more lasting. It makes the section’s later benefit explicitly endure. | terra: Worldly allotments are enjoyment and adornment, whereas what is with God is خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰ, giving the section's delayed promise its lasting scale.
terra: One person meets a good promise while another has only been given present-life enjoyment; this is the section's secured later gift set directly against earlier possession.

luna: The verse says God creates and chooses, while people have no choice, الخيرة. The section’s خ ي ر branch includes choosing between things; this verse marks the boundary of who chooses. | terra: The Lord creates and chooses, while creatures have no ٱلْخِيَرَةُ; this qualifies the section's dictionary sense of choosing the better of two things.

luna: The verse says praise belongs to God in the first life and the Hereafter, then says to Him is the return. It joins the section’s two time-periods to an explicit destination. | terra: لَهُ ٱلْحَمْدُ فِى ٱلْأُولَىٰ وَٱلْءَاخِرَةِ assigns both the first and later realm to God and ends with return to Him.
terra: The command to seek the later abode with what God has already given, without forgetting one's worldly share, holds the two times together without confusing their worth.
terra: Everything perishes except God, judgment belongs to Him, and all return to Him; passing possession and final destination meet in one ayah.
luna: The verse asks whether people see God begin creation and then repeat it. It states the first and later acts together, not merely a general afterlife theme.
terra: After commanding travel to see how creation began, the ayah says God produces ٱلنَّشْأَةَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ, the section's dictionary definition of the later abode as second creation.
terra: Those who demand punishment be hastened are told that an appointed term already governs it and that it will come suddenly.

luna: The verse calls worldly life play and amusement and says the Hereafter’s home is the true life. It makes the later state the enduring reality. | terra: The worldly life is play and diversion, while the later home is described as the true life, making second creation fuller life rather than mere continuation.
terra: The Romans' defeat is the first condition in the reversal whose promised later stages are stated in 30:3–6.
terra: After their defeat, the Romans will prevail, staging a later condition that overturns the earlier one.
terra: لِلَّهِ ٱلْأَمْرُ مِن قَبْلُ وَمِنۢ بَعْدُ gives God the before and after within the promised reversal from Roman defeat to victory.
terra: On the day of the promised reversal believers rejoice in God's help, naming the favorable outcome anticipated by 30:3–4.
terra: وَعْدَ ٱللَّهِ لَا يُخْلِفُ ٱللَّهُ وَعْدَهُۥ seals the timed reversal of 30:2–5 as a promise that delay cannot invalidate.
terra: God begins creation, repeats it, and then people return to Him, ordering origin, second creation, and destination.
terra: The command to glorify God in evening and morning marks two stages of the daily sequence continued in 30:18.
terra: Praise at late day and noon completes the ordered day begun in 30:17, paralleling the section's attention to a named daylight threshold.

luna: God originates creation and repeats it; the return is easy for Him. This directly joins beginning to what follows. | terra: God begins creation and repeats it, and the repeated creation is easier for Him, reinforcing the certainty of the later arising.
terra: Usurious increase does not grow with God, while almsgiving is multiplied, distinguishing apparent present gain from true eventual increase.
terra: A person's later stage returns from strength to weakness and gray hair, showing that “later” alone does not lexically entail “better.”

luna: On the Hour, the criminals swear they stayed no more than an hour. Their short estimate makes the first life recede into a brief interval when its final scene arrives. | terra: When the Hour rises, the guilty swear they stayed no more than an hour, another later vantage from which the earlier duration collapses.
luna: The believers answer the claim in verse 55: they remained until the Resurrection Day by God’s decree, though they did not know. This gives the apparent hour a longer, appointed span.
terra: When believers see the confederates, they identify the sight as the promise of God and His Messenger come true.
terra: Once God and His Messenger decide a matter, believers have no خِيَرَةُ, setting a boundary on the human freedom implied by the choice sense of خير.
terra: The demand to know when the promise will come supplies the impatient question answered by the fixed appointment in 34:30.
terra: The promised appointment is a day from which people can neither delay nor advance by an hour, making the postponed event exact rather than indefinite.

luna: The verse says God defers people until a specified term, after which they cannot delay it. Its postponement and deadline make explicit the appointment implicit in the section’s later gift. | terra: Human beings are deferred to an appointed term rather than seized immediately, making delay a respite before judgment rather than proof of a better outcome.
terra: Deniers ask when the promise will come, the impatient challenge that ends with their recognition after rising in 36:52.
terra: The trumpet is blown and people rush from the graves, staging the arrival immediately before 36:52 identifies it as the old promise.
terra: Those raised from their graves recognize the event as what the Merciful promised and the messengers truthfully announced.
terra: Whomever God grants long life is reversed in creation, another personal later phase that qualifies any automatic equation of sequence with improvement.

luna: When asked who can revive decayed bones, the answer is the One who created them the first time. The first creation is made the ground for a later return. | terra: The One who originated bones the first time will give them life again, making the first creation evidence for the later one.
terra: The blessed speakers say they will suffer only their first death and no punishment, making that first death the passed boundary of their lasting later condition.

luna: The verse follows rain through plants of different colors until they yellow and become debris. It supplies a specific growth-to-end cycle like the section’s crop image, while leaving its afterlife comparison unstated here.
luna: Those before are made to taste disgrace in worldly life, while the punishment of the Hereafter is greater. The later outcome outweighs the earlier one in the opposite, punitive direction.
terra: The people of Paradise say that God fulfilled His promise and gave them the land to inherit, showing the promised gift at receipt.
terra: The condemned acknowledge two deaths and two lives, directly distinguishing repeated life stages when the final outcome has become visible.

luna: The verse calls this world a temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the home of settlement. It directly contrasts the temporary first span with what follows. | terra: This worldly life is temporary enjoyment while the afterlife is دَارُ ٱلْقَرَارِ, the settled home, sharpening the contrast between passing first and abiding later.
terra: Creation proceeds from dust through infancy, maturity, and old age toward an appointed term, a full personal timeline on which earlier and later can be weighed.
terra: The command to be patient because God's promise is true is followed by the same boundary: its realization may be shown now or lie beyond the Prophet's death.
terra: The question whether one cast into the Fire is better than one arriving safe on Resurrection Day makes the final result decide between two cases.
terra: A word that had already gone forth to an appointed term postpones judgment, another instance of delay resting on a prior divine determination.

luna: One who seeks the harvest of the Hereafter has it increased, while one who seeks the world receives some of it without a share in the next life. It makes the two temporal destinations into distinct harvests. | terra: The crop of the afterlife is increased, while one who wants the crop of this world receives some but no later share; the ayah makes temporal choice a harvest.

luna: What people receive is called worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting for believers. It states the passing/remaining distinction alongside the section’s later valuation. | terra: What people are given is worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting for those who trust Him.
terra: Worldly ornament is called mere enjoyment while the afterlife with the Lord belongs to the Godfearing.
terra: Even if God takes the Prophet away, vengeance on the deniers remains secured; 43:42 supplies the alternative of showing him the promise.
terra: The alternative is that the Prophet is shown what the deniers were promised, and God's power over them guarantees either temporal route.
terra: A former people are made predecessors and an example for later peoples, using earlier and later generations as a moral sequence.
terra: Deniers claim there is only the first death and no raising, explicitly rejecting the second creation denoted by the later abode.
terra: The people of Paradise taste no death beyond the first death, so the first death becomes a boundary after which the later life no longer ends.

luna: The verse tells the Prophet to be patient and not hasten punishment; when the promised event is seen, people seem to have stayed only an hour of a day. It joins waiting for what is promised to a compressed reckoning of the earlier time. | terra: The Messenger is told to be patient for what is promised; when people see it, their entire wait seems only an hour of a day.

luna: The verse pairs what has passed before and what comes after—ما تقدم من ذنبك وما تأخر—just before mentioning completion of favor. That is the section’s prior/later pair attached to a completed benefit. | terra: The prophetic address places what preceded and what came later, مَا تَقَدَّمَ ... وَمَا تَأَخَّرَ, immediately before God's completing His favor.

luna: God promises many gains, hastens one for the believers, and holds another gain they could not yet reach within His power. It is a specific promised benefit divided between an immediate portion and a later one. | terra: God promises many future gains and says He has hastened this one, explicitly distinguishing an immediate installment from later promised gifts.
terra: Another gain, not yet within the believers' power, is already encompassed by God; it closely matches fruit still on the branch yet secured.

luna: God confirms the Messenger’s earlier vision and promises entry into the Sacred Mosque, with a near victory placed before it. The verse joins an earlier sign to its later fulfillment for the same addressee. | terra: God makes the Messenger's vision come true and assures future safe entry into the Sacred Mosque, an old image reaching its appointed realization.

luna: The verse pictures tall date palms with clustered fruit. It gives the section’s dictionary image of a palm carrying its crop a concrete Quranic scene; the previous and following verses supply rain and provision.
luna: The verse calls the produce provision for servants and says dead land is revived by it, “thus the emergence.” Its own contribution connects yielded provision to the later return.

luna: The verse asks whether the first creation wearied God, then says people are confused about a new creation. It explicitly connects the first beginning to a later creation. | terra: The question whether God tired at the first creation exposes confusion about a new creation, pairing the first beginning with the disputed later one.
terra: The Prophet is told to be patient and glorify before sunrise and sunset, placing endurance of a delayed promise inside the ordered course of a day.
terra: Night worship and glorification after prostrations continue the daily sequence begun in 50:39 beyond its two solar thresholds.
terra: What people are promised is declared true, preserving certainty before 51:6 identifies the coming judgment.
terra: Judgment is certain to occur, supplying the adverse event guaranteed by the promise of 51:5.
terra: The question whether a human being may have whatever he wishes states the mistaken claim to choice that 53:25 answers by assigning both the later and the first to God.

luna: The verse answers the disbelievers’ wishes by saying the Hereafter and the first life belong to God. It repeats the section’s two-abode pair in a distinct argumentative setting. | terra: Against a human being's wishes in 53:24, ٱلْءَاخِرَةُ وَٱلْأُولَىٰ both belong to God; the two times in the section are therefore gifts under one Owner.
luna: The verse describes one who turns away from remembrance and wants only worldly life. It marks the boundary of choosing the near life alone.
terra: A person's striving will later be seen, so work done in the first interval remains held for disclosure.
terra: The striving shown in 53:40 is then repaid with the fullest recompense, completing the deferred-payment sequence.

luna: The verse says the second creation is upon God. This is the section’s named “second creation” sense of الدار الآخرة. | terra: وَأَنَّ عَلَيْهِ ٱلنَّشْأَةَ ٱلْأُخْرَىٰ assigns the other or later creation to God, directly matching the section's lexical account of the afterlife.

luna: All on earth is described as perishing. This marks the finite end of the first, earthly span against what remains. | terra: Everything upon the earth passes away, stating the vanishing side of the temporal scale completed by what remains in 55:27.

luna: The face of the Lord, possessor of majesty and honor, is said to remain. It supplies the enduring side of the perishing/remaining boundary. | terra: The face of the Lord remains after all earthly beings pass, giving the abiding counterpart to 55:26.

luna: The Garden of the Hereafter has abundant fruit. This connects fruit-bearing to the later life named in the section, though this verse by itself does not describe a harvest time. | terra: Abundant fruit names the provision whose decisive lasting property, being neither cut off nor forbidden, is stated in 56:33.

luna: The fruit is neither cut off nor forbidden. Its unending availability contrasts with the date palm’s finite last harvest and makes the lasting later reward concrete. | terra: The later garden's fruit is neither cut off nor forbidden, turning the section's fruit preserved to harvest into provision without an ending.
terra: ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ وَٱلْءَاخِرِينَ gathers earlier and later human generations into the single appointment specified by 56:50.
terra: This ayah supplies the fixed endpoint for 56:49: both first and later peoples are assembled لَمَجْمُوعُونَ إِلَىٰ مِيقَـٰتِ يَوْمٍۢ مَّعْلُومٍۢ.
luna: God says He has decreed death among people and cannot be outdone. This makes the first life’s endpoint appointed, alongside the section’s later creation and outcome.
luna: The following verse says God can change people’s forms and bring them into an unknown form. It completes the preceding decree of death with the later transformation.

luna: The verse contrasts the known first creation with what follows and asks why people do not remember. It gives the section’s first/later ordering an explicit creation-and-return frame. | terra: ٱلنَّشْأَةَ ٱلْأُولَىٰ names the first creation and asks the hearer to infer the creation that follows it.

luna: God is named the First and the Last, الأول والآخر. The shared pair preserves its temporal relation while applying it to God’s names. | terra: هُوَ ٱلْأَوَّلُ وَٱلْءَاخِرُ makes the First and the Last divine names, setting the section's relative human before and after inside an absolute boundary.
terra: Those who gave before the victory rank above those who gave afterward, yet God has promised both the best; temporal order, degrees, and assured good meet in one ayah.
terra: The one who lends God a good loan is promised multiplication and a noble reward, another contractual image for value held until later.
terra: Men and women who lend God a good loan receive multiplication and a noble reward, repeating the section's deferred-transaction image.

luna: The worldly life is compared to rain-fed growth that flourishes and then yellows and crumbles, before the verse contrasts punishment with forgiveness and approval in the Hereafter. It makes passing yield and final outcome one scene. | terra: A crop pleases its growers, then dries and becomes debris, before the ayah names the later punishment or forgiveness; one visible season stages what passes and what awaits.
terra: Every soul is told to look at what it has sent ahead لِغَدٍۢ, turning tomorrow into the reckoning date of today's investment.
terra: Another favor the believers love is announced as divine help and a near victory, marking a further gift that follows the one already named.

luna: The dying person asks, لولا أخرتني, for a short deferment in which to give charity. The following verse says a soul is not delayed once its appointed term comes; the request makes the section’s deferred-time sense concrete. | terra: At death a person asks for postponement to a near term so he can give, showing the vain wish for one more credit period after its proper time has ended.
terra: God will never postpone a soul once its term arrives, the explicit boundary to every image of payment or fruit carried forward.
terra: A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, framing later divine increase as repayment of a present advance.
terra: سَيَجْعَلُ ٱللَّهُ بَعْدَ عُسْرٍۢ يُسْرًۭا makes ease a divinely promised later phase following present hardship.
terra: God creates death and life to test which people are best in deed, joining life's endpoints to a divine comparison of what is better.

luna: The garden owners swear to cut their crop in the morning, expecting a later yield from what they have kept growing. This is a direct harvest-time scene against the section’s palm whose fruit remains until the final picking. | terra: The garden owners swear they will harvest in the morning, staging an expected crop at a fixed later point whose security proves false.
terra: The garden owners make no reservation when fixing their morning harvest, intensifying the false certainty reversed during the night.

luna: While they sleep, an affliction from their Lord passes over the garden overnight. The verse supplies the intervening delay that turns the planned morning harvest into a lost one. | terra: A visitation circles the garden during the night while its owners sleep, interrupting the interval between their promise and 68:20's ruined morning.

luna: The garden is found as though cut down or blackened. This reverses the section’s image of fruit remaining on the tree through the harvest season. | terra: By morning the garden is stripped dark, the opposite of the section's fruit remaining safely on its tree until harvest.

luna: The owners call one another at daybreak. This is the morning threshold at which the planned harvest is to begin. | terra: At morning the owners call one another, marking the appointed harvest time after the unseen nocturnal loss.

luna: They urge one another to go early to their crop if they mean to reap it. The verse makes the harvest timing explicit. | terra: They set out early to cut the crop if they truly intend to harvest, continuing the expected act whose failure is disclosed in 68:26–27.
luna: They reach the garden early, determined to keep the poor from it. This continues the planned harvest and shows that its expected yield is already treated as secured.

luna: When they see the garden, they think they have lost their way. Their first expectation of a harvest is reversed by the ruined crop. | terra: When the owners finally see the garden they first think they have lost the way, recording the moment expectation meets its altered outcome.

luna: They realize instead that they have been deprived. This names the outcome of a crop they expected to gather later. | terra: They recognize that they have been deprived, the failed harvest serving as a boundary case for the section's secured deferred gift.

luna: After the garden is lost, its owners hope their Lord will replace it with something better, خيرا منها. The verse gives the section’s خ ي ر sense a concrete later compensation after an earlier loss.
luna: The verse says the punishment of the Hereafter is greater than this punishment. It sets the garden’s present loss beside a later consequence.
terra: Deniers are progressively drawn from where they do not know before 68:45 names their respite, distinguishing delay from escape.
terra: God grants respite while His plan remains firm, showing that an outcome can be fully secured even when delay favors the hearer only in appearance.
terra: The people of Paradise are told to eat and drink for what they sent ahead in past days, depicting the delayed payment at the moment it is received.
terra: People see the promised punishment as far away, stating the human perception of delay that 70:7 reverses.
terra: God sees the supposedly distant event as near, exposing the difference between perceived postponement and its true divine measure.

luna: The people are called to worship and forgiveness, and God will defer them to a specified term; once it comes, it cannot be delayed. It joins a promised respite to its fixed end. | terra: God will forgive and postpone people to a named term, but the ayah also marks that the divine term cannot be postponed once it comes.
terra: The Messenger says he does not know whether the promised event is near or whether his Lord has assigned it a long term, explicitly separating certainty from timing.
terra: Whatever good people send ahead they will find with God as better and greater in reward, a precise model of deferred value kept secure.
luna: The oath names the morning as it brightens. This is a precise light-increasing threshold parallel to the section’s post-sunrise sequence.

luna: The verse says the warning is for whoever wishes to advance or lag behind. This directly names the section’s first/later relation as movement forward or backward, with the warning as its boundary. | terra: The warning addresses whoever wishes to advance or lag behind, using the same opposition between preceding and coming later that defines الآخر in the section.
luna: Every soul is then said to be held in pledge for what it earned. This supplies the later accounting that follows the advance/lag choice in verse 37.
terra: On the later Day each person is told what he sent ahead and left behind, بِمَا قَدَّمَ وَأَخَّرَ, so temporal placement becomes disclosed outcome.

luna: The verse says people love the immediate life. It isolates the first side of the contrast completed by the next verse. | terra: تُحِبُّونَ ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ identifies love of the immediate life as the preference whose other side is named in 75:21.

luna: The verse says they leave the Hereafter. Together with verse 20, it names the contrary choice to the section’s better-later weighing. | terra: وَتَذَرُونَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ completes 75:20: the later is abandoned precisely because the immediate is preferred.

luna: People love the immediate life and leave behind a heavy day. This is an explicit preference for the near term over the later one, contrary to the section’s valuation. | terra: Those who love ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ leave behind a weighty future Day, a direct instance of choosing the nearer time over a consequential later one.
terra: What the hearers are promised will certainly occur, a bare assurance whose content is judgment rather than gift.
terra: The destruction of ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ gives the first generation an adverse end rather than a better continuation.
terra: ثُمَّ نُتْبِعُهُمُ ٱلْءَاخِرِينَ makes the later generations follow the former in judgment, reversing 93:4's favorable relation between later and first.

luna: God makes night dark and brings out its duha, ضحاها. It directly locates the morning brightness named in the section against the preceding night. | terra: وَأَخْرَجَ ضُحَىٰهَا depicts God bringing out the sky's morning brightness, the growing-light feature developed in the section.
luna: The transgressor who prefers the worldly life is introduced before the statement that Hell is his home. It names the choice reversed by the section’s better-later measure.
luna: The one who fears standing before the Lord and restrains desire is introduced before the Garden outcome. This is a specific stance toward the later life.
luna: The Garden is said to be the home of the person described in verse 40. It completes the choice-and-outcome contrast.

luna: The Hour makes their whole stay seem no more than an evening or its duha. The verse uses the exact morning-time word developed in the section as a measure for a life viewed from its end. | terra: At resurrection the whole earlier stay seems no longer than an evening or its ضُحَىٰ, turning the section's unfinished morning interval into a measure of vanished first life.
luna: The oath names the night as it departs. This gives the dark side of the transition completed by the next verse’s breathing morning.
luna: The oath names the morning as it breathes. That image matches the section’s light increasing at a threshold after sunrise.
terra: At the cosmic ending every soul learns مَا قَدَّمَتْ وَأَخَّرَتْ, another exact joining of what was advanced and deferred with its final reckoning.

luna: The verse says God originates and repeats. Its concise pair matches the section’s ordering of first and later acts. | terra: God begins and repeats creation, a compact formulation of the first origin followed by renewed creation.

luna: The verse says God brings out pasture before the following verse says it becomes dark debris; the same surah later says the Hereafter is better and more lasting. It stages the crop’s earlier flourishing against its later end.
luna: The pasture becomes dark debris. This is the plant-life boundary between a season’s growth and its ending, near the surah’s explicit contrast of the near life with the lasting Hereafter.

luna: The preceding verse says people prefer the nearer life. It supplies the opposing choice that makes the next verse’s better and more lasting Hereafter a reversal. | terra: Preferring ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا states the mistaken choice to which 87:17 answers that the afterlife is better and more lasting.

luna: The verse states that the Hereafter is better and more lasting, matching the section’s explicit weighing of later against earlier. | terra: The formula ٱلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰ repeats the section's judgment that the later is better and adds the reason that it lasts.

luna: At the end, a person regrets not having sent deeds ahead for “my life.” The verse makes the earlier opportunity and later reckoning one concrete sequence. | terra: At judgment a person wishes he had sent something ahead for his true life, naming the later existence as the life for which the first should have prepared.
terra: The satisfied soul is commanded to return to its Lord, joining attained رضا to the final place of return.

luna: The oath is by the sun and its duha, ضحاها. The section’s dictionary entry for ض ح و names the bright time after sunrise, so the verse shares its precise sunlit interval. | terra: The oath by the sun and ضُحَىٰهَا parallels 93:1's oath while making the brightening associated with that time explicit.
terra: The moon follows the sun, adding succession to the solar-brightness oath of 91:1.
terra: The day reveals the sun, further defining the illumination staged by the ضُحَىٰ oath in 91:1.
